blocks.text: 1. PReLU

blocks.alt: Alpha gets learned during training, forming PReLU

blocks.text: Leaky ReLU's fixed leak size, chosen manually before training even starts, left one more genuine question open. PReLU asks a genuinely different question: why not let the network learn that leak size itself, rather than fixing it by hand ahead of time?
PReLU, short for Parametric ReLU, is one more variant in the same ReLU family covered across this module, building directly on the exact idea already introduced in the Leaky ReLU topic.
2. PReLU's Mathematics

PReLU takes any real number as input and asks the exact same question ReLU and Leaky ReLU both ask: is this input positive? If yes, it outputs the input unchanged, exactly like both of those earlier functions already covered in this module.

If the input is zero or negative, it outputs alpha times the input, exactly the same formula as Leaky ReLU, except alpha is now a genuinely learned parameter rather than a fixed, manually chosen constant.

blocks.text: 3. Learned Versus Fixed

blocks.alt: Leaky ReLU has a fixed alpha while PReLU has a learned alpha

blocks.text: This connects back to the slope parameter already covered in the Leaky ReLU topic. Leaky ReLU's alpha is fixed, chosen once before training even starts, always exactly 0.01 for instance, for every single neuron, for the entire training run.

PReLU's alpha is instead learned, adjusted during training exactly like any other weight, directly connecting back to Weights and Biases, already covered in the Neural Network Fundamentals module, treating this leak size as just one more learnable parameter rather than a fixed hyperparameter.
4. Per-Neuron Flexibility

blocks.alt: Each neuron gets its own alpha value

blocks.text: Each neuron, or sometimes each entire layer depending on the specific implementation, gets its own separate, individually learned alpha value. One neuron might genuinely learn a leak close to Leaky ReLU's common 0.01 default.

Another neuron might learn a genuinely different leak entirely, 0.3 for instance, if that value actually works better for whatever specific role that particular neuron ends up playing. The network discovers what actually works best for each specific neuron, rather than every neuron being forced to share the exact same fixed value.
5. A Genuinely Small Parameter Addition

blocks.alt: PReLU adds very few extra parameters

blocks.text: This connects back to the total parameter count already covered in the Weights and Biases topic. Each learned alpha is one more parameter added to the network, on top of every weight and bias already counted in that earlier topic.

This is a genuinely small addition relative to a network's total weight and bias count, since there is only ever one alpha per neuron or per layer, considerably fewer than the many individual weights that same neuron or layer already has.
6. How Alpha Actually Gets Trained

This connects back to backpropagation, covered in its own full, dedicated module later in this course. Alpha gets updated through the exact same gradient-based process as every other weight in the network, with no special, separate training procedure needed at all.

This means PReLU fits directly into the existing training loop already covered throughout this course, requiring no genuinely new machinery, simply one more learnable value flowing through the same forward and backward passes every other parameter already goes through.
7. When PReLU's Extra Flexibility Genuinely Pays Off

Large datasets, where there is genuinely enough data to reliably learn good alpha values for every individual neuron, are where PReLU's extra flexibility genuinely pays off, since the added flexibility has enough real signal available to actually be worth learning correctly.

Small datasets carry a genuine risk instead, where the extra learned parameters can risk overfitting, covered in further depth in the Regularization Techniques module later in this course, since there may not be enough data to reliably learn good, generalizable alpha values for every single neuron.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: PReLU is not automatically better than Leaky ReLU. Its extra learned flexibility is a genuine tradeoff, worth the added complexity mainly when there is sufficient data to actually benefit from it.

blocks.text: 8. The ReLU Family, So Far

blocks.alt: The ReLU family includes ReLU, leaky ReLU, and PReLU

blocks.text: The ReLU family covered across this module so far includes plain ReLU, the simplest, fastest to compute, but genuinely risking dying neurons, and Leaky ReLU, which fixes dying neurons using one extra, fixed hyperparameter.

PReLU, covered fully in this topic, also fixes dying neurons, but adapts its leak per individual neuron and adds genuinely learned, rather than fixed, parameters, the most flexible, and most complex, of the three variants covered so far.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When PReLU Is Genuinely Worth It

blocks.alt: A large dataset with enough compute points toward trying PReLU

blocks.text: A large dataset, where Leaky ReLU's fixed leak already shows real, measurable benefit, is a genuine case where PReLU's learned flexibility can often push performance further still, given enough data to actually learn good, individualized alpha values reliably.

A small dataset, or a quick prototype where iteration speed matters more than squeezing out the last bit of performance, often finds Leaky ReLU's simpler, fixed choice genuinely sufficient, without needing PReLU's added complexity and overfitting risk.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly compares Leaky ReLU's fixed alpha against a simulated PReLU where alpha varies per neuron, illustrating the per-neuron flexibility covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

def leaky_relu(x, alpha=0.01):
    return np.where(x > 0, x, alpha * x)

def prelu(x, alphas):
    # alphas: one learned value per neuron, simulating what training would produce
    return np.where(x > 0, x, alphas * x)

negative_inputs = np.array([-3.0, -3.0, -3.0, -3.0])  # same negative input, 4 different neurons

fixed_alpha = 0.01
leaky_outputs = leaky_relu(negative_inputs, alpha=fixed_alpha)
print(f"Leaky ReLU (fixed alpha={fixed_alpha}): {leaky_outputs}")

# Simulating 4 different neurons, each having learned its own alpha during training
learned_alphas = np.array([0.01, 0.15, 0.05, 0.30])
prelu_outputs = prelu(negative_inputs, learned_alphas)
print(f"PReLU (learned per-neuron alphas): {prelu_outputs}")
print(f"Learned alphas themselves: {learned_alphas}")
print("\nNotice every Leaky ReLU output uses the same fixed leak, while PReLU's outputs vary,")
print("reflecting each neuron's own individually learned leak size")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The learned_alphas array in this example simulates what backpropagation would actually produce after real training, each neuron converging on whatever leak size genuinely works best for its own specific role.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: PReLU lets the network learn its own leak size, rather than fixing it by hand like Leaky ReLU.
It uses the exact same formula as Leaky ReLU, but alpha is a learned parameter, not a fixed constant.
Alpha is adjusted during training exactly like any other weight, via the standard backpropagation process.
Each neuron, or layer, gets its own individually learned alpha, letting the network discover what works best per neuron.
Each learned alpha adds one small additional parameter, a modest addition to a network's total parameter count.
Large datasets, with enough signal to learn good alphas, are where PReLU's flexibility genuinely pays off.
Small datasets risk overfitting these extra learned parameters, where Leaky ReLU's simpler, fixed choice often suffices.
The ReLU family so far: ReLU simplest, Leaky ReLU fixed leak, PReLU learned, per-neuron leak.
Next up: ELU, a genuinely different fix for negative inputs, using a smooth curve instead of a straight line.
